newsitem.title: THAILAND: Top Thai finance firms said turning down deposits.
newsitem.headline: Top Thai finance firms said turning down deposits.

text.p: A surfeit of cash is forcing some leading Thai finance firms to turn away depositors wanting to buy promissory notes, finance executives said on Friday.
"Sometimes we have had to refuse because we have excess liquidity," First Vice-President Oranuch Apisaksirikul at TISCO Plc told Reuters.
"It is not like a deadline where we say, 'okay, today we don't take promissory notes.' It depends on the rate, and the amount and our situation," she said.
Thailand's financial sector was rocked earlier this week when the Bank of Thailand took the unprecedented step of naming 10 ailing finance firms and ordered them to raise capital.
The central bank also set stringent new loan provisioning requirements for all finance companies and banks, to cover sub-standard loans to the depressed property sector.
The tough government measures and concerns about stability of troubled financial institutions sparked a run on billions of baht in deposits at the firms perceived as weak.
Many depositors had attempted to make deposits instead with blue chip finance companies, the executives said.
With Thai finance firms paying around 11 percent interest on three-month promissory notes, accepting more new deposits could raise overall funding costs and cut margins at large firms, they said.

"We are not issuing promissory notes today because we have so much money at the moment, and are unlikely to do so on Monday and Tuesday," said a senior officer at Krungthai Thanakit's treasury department.

"I don't think you can make sweeping conclusions about any individual firm on any one day issuing or not issuing notes. But the conclusion you could draw is that there has been a definite flight to quality," said Richard Henderson, head of research at Krungthai Thanakit.

Under conditions of excess liquidity, decisions to issue notes to depositors depends on factors such as the firm's underlying financing costs, the balance of its liabilities, the maturity of other instruments the company holds and needs to cover, and individual cash needs for projects firms may have ongoing, analysts said.

But investment options for finance firms accepting deposits are limited by a slump in the Thai stock market, which has sunk to more than 4-1/2 year lows, interbank lending rates in single digits, low loan demand in Thailand's high-interest environmemt and the slowing economy, analysts said.

Penalties for early withdrawal of notes were not discouraging since depositors withdrawing six-month notes still received three month rates that differ by around only 50 basis points, executives said.
Other leading finance firms Asia Credit Plc and Phatra Thanakit Plc said they were continuing to accept all deposits, but were monitoring the situation closely.

"We have seen a lot of new customers recently, particularly this week. We can continue to make money on promissory note deposits at the moment on short-term bank paper and government bonds," said a senior executive at Phatra Thanakit.

"We want to remain flexible and are comfortable with our liquidity situation at the moment. We cut PN rates last month and there is a possibility that we could do so again, though we want to remain competitive with bank deposits rates," he said.
